newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - UBS joins CA bidding, shop king adds mystery.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UBS joins CA bidding, shop king adds mystery.

text.p: A surprise third bidder widened the field in the race for Creditanstalt on Monday as Austria's finance ministry reported Union Bank of Switzerland had joined a group led by EA-Generali.
Karl Wlaschek, 79-year-old doyen of the Austrian retail industry, emerged as the mystery contender in the fight for control of the country's most traditional bank.
Meanwhile, UBS strengthened EA-Generali's arm by enabling it to bid for the government's entire 70 percent voting stake with a view to placing a good quarter of it on the market later.
Market leader Bank Austria, which took the staid Viennese financial scene by storm last week when it unveiled its bid, also submitted a firm offer ahead of the 0700 GMT deadline.
"We will now carefully evaluate all the bids in order to find the best possible solution," the finance ministry said.
Finance Minister Viktor Klima, forecasting a decision by the end of the year, expressed delight that the sale of the state's 19.9 million shares would bring a windfall.
"My aim is to get the most attractive price and we already have one clear victor -- the Austrian taxpayer," he said.
At the current market price of 736 schillings, the government's Creditanstalt stake is worth around 14.5 billion schillings ($1.3 billion).
But Klima will be hoping to net more than that.
Bank Austria is reportedly willing to pay 16 billion schillings or 804 schillings for each ordinary voting share.

Entrepreneur Wlaschek, 79, is not short of cash either after making around 15 billion schillings from the sale of his Billa supermarket chain to Germany's Rewe in July. He too has bid for the state's entire holding.

The EA-Generali consortium, which includes Germany's Commerzbank, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Austrian savings bank Die Erste Oesterreichische SparCasse (First Austrian), also put in a strong finish.
Union Bank of Switzerland joined Commerzbank, Belgium's Bacob, Banca Commerciale and First Austrian in helping the group to find the extra cash needed to bid for all the government's shares.
The "core consortium" would take control of 74 percent of the state's stake.
A second group, including UBS, would take on the remaining 26 percent with a view to placing the shares over the stock exchange, an EA-Generali spokesman explained.
UBS confirmed it would act as global coordinator for the placement.

According to the finance ministry, the consortium would carve up the basic 74 percent as follows: 40 percent Austrian companies and individuals, eight percent Austrian subsidiaries of foreign companies and 52 percent foreign companies.
"The core consortium has bid for 74 percent (of the state's stake) and will place the remaining 26 percent on the market," EA-Generali spokesman Josef Hlinka told Reuters.
"UBS is part of the placement consortium and will not be involved in a possible long-term solution," he added.

Analysts welcomed the consortium's beefed-up bid and forecast a closely fought contest with Bank Austria. Wlaschek added an interesting twist but was unlikely to succeed in his foray into banking, most agreed.
"The government is unlikely to sell to a private individual," said Victoria Maxwell at James Capel in London.
"Between them the members of the consortium have the money and they can keep pushing up their bid and give Bank Austria a run for its money." ($1=10.93 Schilling)
